operations.evidence: Relevant landlords must ensure at least one smoke alarm is equipped on each storey containing a room used as living accommodation.
The rule does not specify that one alarm is adequate for every layout or risk profile.
A carbon-monoxide alarm is required in each living-accommodation room containing a fixed combustion appliance, excluding gas cookers.
Appliance presence and room use must be established for the specific property.
Landlords must repair or replace prescribed smoke and carbon-monoxide alarms after being informed and finding that they are faulty.
A tenant report alone does not establish the technical fault or completion of repair.
Local housing authorities enforce the alarm requirements.
Enforcement responsibility does not mean action has occurred at a named property.
A local authority can impose a civil penalty of up to £5,000 where a landlord fails to comply with a remedial notice.
The statutory ceiling is not evidence that a breach or penalty exists.
The regulations do not stipulate the exact position of smoke or carbon-monoxide alarms.
Absence of a prescribed position does not remove the need for effective installation.
Landlords should follow individual manufacturer instructions when installing alarms.
Manufacturer guidance must be matched to the actual alarm model.
The guidance generally recommends smoke alarms on the ceiling in circulation spaces such as halls or landings.
This general recommendation is not a substitute for model-specific instructions or risk assessment.
The guidance generally recommends carbon-monoxide alarms at head height and approximately one to three metres from a potential source.
The general distance should not override manufacturer-specific requirements.
Tenants are advised to replace batteries during a tenancy, while landlords remain responsible for repairing or replacing faulty alarms.
Responsibility can depend on whether a battery change resolves the fault.
Specialist alarms using vibration or flashing lights may be required for residents who are deaf or hard of hearing.
A resident's accessibility needs must not be inferred from property data.
Heat detectors are not a replacement for smoke alarms under the guidance.
A heat detector may still form part of a wider fire-safety system.
Landlords must check prescribed alarms are in proper working order on the day a new tenancy begins.
The duty does not establish that a documented test occurred for a specific tenancy.

The guidance lists exclusions including landlord-shared accommodation, long leases, student halls, hotels, refuges, care homes, hospitals, hospices and certain low-cost ownership or healthcare accommodation.
An exclusion must be verified from the legal tenancy and use, not inferred from building type.
The small-block guide covers qualifying purpose-built or later-compliant converted blocks limited to three storeys and no more than six flats.
Buildings outside the stated design and size scope require other guidance.
The guide applies to common parts as well as the building structure, external walls and doors between flats and common parts.
Scope under fire law is not evidence that those elements are compliant.
Potential responsible persons include social housing providers, private landlords, freeholders, resident management companies, right-to-manage companies and managing agents.
The actual responsible person must be established from control and legal arrangements.
Responsible persons should complete and maintain a suitable fire risk assessment for the premises within scope.
The existence or quality of an assessment cannot be inferred from the building category.
The guide is based on qualifying blocks designed around a stay-put strategy.
A stay-put strategy must not be assumed where design or compartmentation differs materially.
Under the described stay-put approach, occupants of the flat where fire occurs should evacuate.
Real incidents may require different action based on conditions and fire-service instructions.
Occupants of other flats are normally safe to remain unless their flat is affected by fire or smoke or the fire and rescue service instructs them to leave.
The guidance does not guarantee safety in every incident or building.
A stay-put strategy does not prevent occupants from leaving if they choose and can do so safely.
Leaving through smoke-affected common parts may increase risk.
Adequate fire-resisting compartmentation is essential to support the stay-put strategy.
Original design intent does not prove that compartmentation remains intact.
The guide assumes a low probability of fire in common parts and that any such fire is limited in extent.
The assumption is a design basis, not an observed condition for a particular block.
Responsible persons should ensure contractors are competent, while ultimate responsibility for compliance remains with the responsible person.
Certification can support competence checks but does not guarantee compliant work.
The Fire Safety Act clarified that fire-risk assessments cover building structure, external walls and individual flat entrance doors between dwellings and common parts.
Legal coverage does not establish the physical condition of those elements.
More than one Responsible Person may exist within the same building where different parties control workplaces or fire-safety matters.
The allocation of duties requires building-specific legal and operational evidence.
The Fire Safety (England) Regulations introduced additional duties for medium-rise and high-rise blocks, including information and safety-measure requirements.
Height classification and applicable duties must be verified from reliable building data.
The Home Office describes its responsibilities guidance as a high-level, non-exhaustive summary.
Premises-specific risk assessment and legal advice may be needed; the summary must not be used as a complete compliance determination.
